paper.title: Intelligent Prediction of WHO/ISUP Grade in Clear-Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Using CT-Based Fusion Delta Features: A Multicenter Study with Biological Interpretability Exploration.
paper.abstract:
Rationale And Objectives: Our study aimed to develop a delta deep learning radiomics model for predicting World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grade in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and to find relevant biomarkers and explore the potential biological mechanisms.
Material And Methods: This multicenter cohort of 754 patients with ccRCC from five hospitals was split into training and internal validation cohorts in a 7:3 ratio, along with an external validation cohort (n=221) from three other hospitals. Radiomics and deep learning features were extracted from the tumor regions on multiphase contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT). Delta features were calculated as the absolute differences between features from different imaging phases. The selected features were used to develop delta deep learning radiomics signatures using different classifiers. The diagnostic performance in each model was assessed. Furthermore, gene expression profiling was conducted to for exploratory analysis of biological correlates associated with the model's grade predictions.
Results: The delta model achieved AUCs of 0.736 (95% CI 0.671-0.801) and 0.701 (95% CI 0.635-0.768) in the internal and external validation cohorts, respectively, which were numerically higher than those of the original model based on traditional deep learning radiomics features and demographic baseline clinical model. Additionally, the delta model demonstrated good calibration and a higher net benefit. Bioinformatics and multiomics analysis revealed that high-grade risk-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with inflammation-related pathways, providing preliminary exploratory biological insights into the model's predictions.
Conclusion: The delta model demonstrated promising performance in WHO/ISUP grade. DEGs in predicted high-grade ccRCC were associated with inflammation-related pathways.

paper.title: CT-based radiomics for interpretable outcome prediction after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a multicenter cohort study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Prognostic assessment after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) mainly relies on clinical variables and computed tomography (CT) findings, but current models often lack biological interpretability. We developed and validated a clinical-radiomics prognostic model and subsequently performed exploratory cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomic characterization of model-defined risk phenotypes.
Methods: This multicenter cohort from the PROSAH-MPC registry included 879 patients across four hospitals. Patients from the primary center were split into training (n = 637) and internal validation (n = 160) cohorts, while patients from three other centers formed an external validation cohort (n = 82). Admission CT hemorrhagic lesions were automatically segmented using the validated BrainHemoAI platform, and radiomic features were extracted with PyRadiomics. Clinical, radiomics, and combined clinical-radiomics XGBoost models were developed and interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Risk scores from the clinical-radiomics model were applied to an independent prospective enrichment, gene setCSF​ proteomic cohort to define combined model-based high- and low-risk groups. Gene Ontology (GO)/ Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), and protein-protein interaction (PPI) analyses were performed.
Results: The combined model yielded AUCs of 0.892 and 0.820 in the internal test and external validation cohorts, respectively. Risk reclassification analyses suggested that radiomic features may provide complementary prognostic information. SHAP identified radiomic heterogeneity and key clinical variables as major predictors. Meanwhile, exploratory CSF proteomic analysis identified candidate differentially expressed proteins and associated pathway signals that differed between groups defined by high and low combined clinical-radiomics risk scores.
Conclusions: This clinical-radiomics prognostic model enables accurate outcome prediction and provides exploratory biological insight into unfavorable recovery after aSAH, supporting refined risk stratification and potential targeted therapeutic development.
Trial Registration: PROSAH-MPC. NCT05738083. Registered 16 November 2022 - Retrospectively registered, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05738083 .

paper.title: Distinguishing nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease from pulmonary tuberculosis using visual machine learning: a Chinese multicenter prospective surveillance cohort study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are opportunistic pathogens. In recent years, the incidence of NTM diseases has increased significantly worldwide. Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (NTM-PD) is highly similar to pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) in clinical presentation, imaging features, and sputum smear microscopy results, which can easily cause misdiagnosis. Notably, there are significant differences between the anti-infective treatment regimens for NTM-PD and PTB; however, effective differential diagnostic methods are currently lacking, seriously limiting the standardized treatment of NTM diseases.
Objective: This study aimed to distinguish NTM-PD from PTB using a visual machine learning approach.
Methods: This study employed a prospective cohort design to conduct prospective national surveillance of NTM-PD in 17 hospitals participating in the China Non-Tuberculous Mycobacteria Surveillance (CNTMS). A total of 6694 patients were included in the analysis, NTM-PD was considered a positive event. Visual models based on logistic regression (LR) and a gradient boosting framework using tree-based learning algorithms (LightGBM, LGB) were developed using important predictive features such as bronchiectasis, diabetes, and geographic region. Model performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the curve (AUC). Model predictions were interpreted using SHAP (a method that explains which features drive each prediction).
Results: Nine characteristics, including bronchodilation, diabetes, HIV, etc., were screened as key variables for distinguish NTM-PD and PTB. The AUC values of Logistic regression and LightGBM models in the training set were 0.714 (95%CI: 0.679 ~ 0.749) and 0.862 (95%CI: 0.843 ~ 0.882), respectively. In the two external test sets, the average AUC values of logistic regression model and LightGBM model were 0.789 (95%CI: 0.728-0.851) and 0.798 (95%CI: 0.743-0.851), respectively. Nomogram visualization identified bronchiectasis, HIV infection, COPD, and geographic region as the major contributors to the predictive score. SHAP visualization revealed geographic region, diabetes, and occupation as the most influential features for model prediction.
Conclusions: Logistic regression and LGB models demonstrated effective accuracy and stability in external validation, and their visualization and interpretability analyses provide auxiliary evidence for the rapid clinical differentiation between NTM-PD and PTB.

paper.title: Integrating Intratumoral and Peritumoral Features via a Cross-Attention Transformer on Super-resolution MRI for Glioblastoma Survival Risk Stratification: A Multicenter Study.
paper.abstract:
Rationale And Objectives: To develop and validate a Cross-Region Transformer using super-resolution (SR) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to integrate intratumoral and peritumoral features for overall survival (OS) prediction in glioblastoma.
Materials And Methods: This multicenter study included 362 patients (training, n = 228; internal test, n = 57; external validation, n = 77). Preoperative contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI underwent generative adversarial network-based SR reconstruction. Intratumoral and 10-mm peritumoral features were extracted using 2.5D convolutional neural networks and fused by asymmetric cross-attention to generate a deep learning-based risk score (DLRS), which was combined with independent clinical factors. Performance was evaluated using C-index, time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analysis, calibration, decision curve analysis, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping, and SHapley Additive exPlanations.
Results: The Cross-Region Transformer achieved C-indices of 0.787 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.734-0.840), 0.711 (95% CI, 0.593-0.829), and 0.726 (95% CI, 0.627-0.826) in the training, internal test, and external validation cohorts, respectively, with numerically higher discrimination than single-region and feature-concatenation models. The combined clinical-DLRS model, incorporating the Stupp regimen, number of lesions, Ki-67 index, and DLRS, achieved corresponding C-indices of 0.836 (95% CI, 0.788-0.884), 0.742 (95% CI, 0.628-0.855), and 0.754 (95% CI, 0.658-0.850). The DLRS significantly stratified OS in external validation (median, 7.5 vs 23.5 months; P < 0.001). Interpretability analyses highlighted enhancing margins within the necrotic core and the intratumoral-peritumoral interface.
Conclusion: The Cross-Region Transformer integrates complementary intratumoral and peritumoral representations from SR MRI. The resulting interpretable DLRS supports noninvasive survival prediction and risk stratification in glioblastoma.

paper.title: Identifying sepsis treatment response subtypes and personalized bundles via causal machine learning.
paper.abstract:
Objective: To identify sepsis treatment response subtypes and derive personalized bundles using causal machine learning (CML).
Methods: We conducted a retrospective multicenter study using the ICU-HAI registry from West China Hospital and the MIMIC-IV 3.0 database from the United States. Patients with sepsis in the ICU-HAI were assigned to development and internal validation cohorts. In the development cohort, CML algorithms were applied to estimate individual treatment effects (ITE)s of candidate interventions, and the optimal model was selected based on the adjusted Qini statistic. We then identified treatment response subtypes using latent profile analysis of ITEs and derived subtype-specific personalized bundles using LASSO regression. The stability of treatment response subtypes and the effectiveness of the personalized bundles were first evaluated in the internal validation cohort. A LightGBM-based model was developed for subtype prediction and deployed as an online tool which were then applied to the MIMIC cohort for external validation, and bundle effectiveness was further assessed for generalizability.
Results: Among 39,586 sepsis patients from ICU-HAI, three treatment response subtypes were identified. All subtypes shared hemodynamic support strategies. Subtype 1 (younger, lower severity) showed greater responsiveness to epinephrine and corticosteroids, whereas subtype 2 (older with renal impairment) and subtype 3 (cardiovascular comorbidities) were more associated with metabolic stabilization and fluid resuscitation, respectively. The subtype prediction model demonstrated high discriminative performance (AUROC 0.84-0.93). In the internal validation cohort, bundle adherence was associated with lower ICU mortality, with an OR (95% CI) of 0.34 (0.28, 0.41), with consistent findings in the external validation cohort (N = 33,253), with an OR (95% CI) of 0.25 (0.23, 0.28). The marginal structural model using 30-day mortality as the outcome yielded consistent associations.
Conclusions: Leveraging electronic health record data to estimate ITEs identifies distinct treatment response subtypes in sepsis. Tailoring treatment bundles to these specific subtypes may offer advantages over uniform care strategies and holds promise for improving clinical outcomes. Ultimately, this approach outlines a scalable framework for precision sepsis care, though these findings warrant prospective validation.

paper.title: Integrated radiomics-deep learning modeling of hepatic vasculature for enhanced noninvasive prediction of portal hypertension and high-risk gastroesophageal varices.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: To evaluate whether CT-derived radiomics and deep learning features can improve non-invasive risk stratification of clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) and high-risk gastroesophageal varices (HRVs) in cirrhotic patients.
Materials And Methods: This retrospective study included 454 cirrhotic patients from center A and 77 from center B. CSPH labels were available only for patients from center A. Patients in both centers with available endoscopic findings were classified as HRVs or non-HRVs. A dual-path modeling framework integrating radiomics and deep learning-derived features extracted from multiple major hepatic vessels was developed, and was compared with single-path (radiomics-only and deep learning-only), single-vessel, vascular geometric, and clinical-feature-based models. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
Results: For CSPH prediction, the dual-path model achieved the highest AUC (0.892 vs. 0.678-0.870 for the other models; P < 0.05 for most comparisons). For HRVs prediction, the proposed model achieved AUCs of 0.790 and 0.782 in the internal and external test set, respectively. The proposed model consistently outperformed the single-path models (0.625-0.648; all P < 0.05), single-vessel models (0.526-0.642; all P < 0.05), the vascular geometric model (0.528; P < 0.01), and the clinical-feature-based models (0.327-0.728; P < 0.001 for the APRI-based model) in the external test set.
Conclusion: A dual-path model integrating multi-vessel radiomics and deep learning features demonstrates robust predictive performance for CSPH and HRVs in cirrhotic patients. This approach may provide a new non-invasive alternative for risk stratification and clinical management of portal hypertension-related complications.

paper.title: Multicenter CT-Based Deep Learning for Preoperative Nodal Risk Stratification in Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma.
paper.abstract:
Background: Accurate preoperative risk stratification for lymph node metastasis (LNM) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) remains difficult. We developed and validated ThyLNT, a Transformer-based 2.5D deep learning model using preoperative computed tomography (CT), and explored related biological features in multi-omics analyses.
Methods: A total of 1560 patients with PTC from six hospitals were retrospectively included. The Tongji Hospital cohort was divided into training and internal validation sets, and five external cohorts were used for independent testing. Seven 2.5D tumor slices were extracted per patient, encoded with a DenseNet201 backbone, and fused by a Transformer. Model performance was compared with radiomics, ensemble learning, and multi-instance learning using AUC, calibration, decision curve, and precision-recall analyses. Bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics were used to explore related biological features.
Results: ThyLNT achieved an AUC of 0.882 (CI, 0.858-0.905) in the training cohort, 0.787 (CI, 0.738-0.835) in the internal validation cohort, and 0.772 (CI, 0.662-0.878) to 0.827 (CI, 0.763-0.885) across the five external cohorts. It showed multicenter discrimination, whereas calibration and threshold-dependent operating characteristics varied across cohorts. Multi-omics analyses provided exploratory biological context, including candidate associations with vascular endothelial growth factor A-related signaling and lipid metabolism.
Conclusions: ThyLNT demonstrated multicenter performance for preoperative LNM prediction in PTC and may support risk stratification, although calibration, threshold use, and clinical utility require prospective validation.

paper.title: Machine learning models based on artificial intelligence-derived CT quantitative parameters and CT semantic features for predicting the invasive risk of subsolid pulmonary nodules: a dual-center study.
paper.abstract:
Purpose: To develop and validate machine learning (ML) models integrating artificial intelligence (AI)-derived quantitative CT parameters and CT semantic features for predicting the invasiveness risk of subsolid pulmonary nodules (SSNs).
Materials And Methods: This retrospective dual-center study enrolled 833 patients with surgically resected, pathologically confirmed adenocarcinoma-spectrum SSNs (training, n=586; external validation, n=247). Low risk was defined as atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (AAH), adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (MIA); high risk as invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC). The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) selected features from 19 AI parameters, 7 semantic features, and 3 clinical characteristics. Seven ML models were built and validated using ten-fold cross-validation and external validation. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provided interpretability.
Results: LASSO identified nine predictors (margin, spiculation, lobulation, pleural indentation, vascular convergence, long diameter, solid component ratio, skewness, entropy). In internal cross-validation, all seven models showed comparable performance (mean AUC 0.935-0.940). In external validation, random forest (RF) showed the numerically highest AUC (0.959, 95% CI: 0.938-0.980), although pairwise DeLong tests with Bonferroni correction showed no statistically significant differences among models. SHAP analysis identified long diameter, skewness, spiculation, entropy, and solid component ratio as the top five predictors contributing to invasive risk. An online tool based on RF was deployed at https://subsolid-nodule.shinyapps.io/data/ for real-time individual risk calculation.
Conclusion: Ensemble learning models, particularly RF, integrating AI-derived CT quantitative parameters and CT semantic features accurately predict SSN invasive risk. This non-invasive tool may provide additional information for preoperative risk stratification and multidisciplinary assessment.

paper.title: MelaResNet-34: An enhanced transfer learning model for automated and accurate melanoma diagnosis.
paper.abstract:
Background: Melanoma is an aggressive skin cancer requiring early diagnosis. However, manual diagnostic procedures utilizing dermoscopes are heavily dependent on clinical expertise and are inherently susceptible to high inter-observer subjectivity. Therefore, developing efficient and objective automated auxiliary diagnostic models remains of great clinical value.
Methods: We proposed MelaResNet-34, a transfer learning-based model for automated melanoma detection. Using the ISIC 2019 dataset, we applied data cleaning and moderate augmentation. The ResNet-34 backbone was optimized via a tailored fine-tuning strategy. Following a strict 7.5:2.5 internal split, performance was evaluated using comprehensive metrics (Accuracy, AUC, F1-score, MCC). Crucially, external validation was conducted on the independent PH2 dataset.
Results: Internally, MelaResNet-34 achieved 97.76% accuracy, 0.987 AUC, and an MCC of 0.955, demonstrating highly competitive performance against both classic baselines and contemporary state-of-the-art architectures. Ablation experiments verified the essential roles of transfer learning and moderate augmentation. Furthermore, external validation on the PH2 dataset confirmed robust generalizability (91.0% accuracy, 0.938 AUC) despite inter-institutional domain shifts.
Conclusion: MelaResNet-34 exhibits superior classification and generalization capabilities, highlighting its potential to serve as an efficient, objective diagnostic tool for clinicians. While current results are promising, future large-scale, multi-center prospective validation is required before routine clinical implementation.

paper.title: An interpretable machine learning model for predicting intensive care unit mortality risk in elderly patients with concomitant cardiogenic shock and sepsis: Development and external validation using two large critical care databases.
paper.abstract:
Introduction: Older adults with concomitant cardiogenic shock (CS) and sepsis represent a high-risk mixed-shock population in whom early prognosis is difficult. We aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine-learning model for ICU mortality.
Methods: Patients aged ≥65 years with concomitant CS and sepsis were identified from MIMIC-IV v3.1 (n=1,219) and eICU-CRD v2.0 (n=166). MIMIC-IV was stratified 70:30 into training (n=853) and internal validation (n=366), while eICU-CRD was reserved for external validation. Feature selection used the intersection of Boruta and LASSO in the training cohort. Ten models were tuned by stratified 5-fold cross-validation; the primary model family was selected by the highest mean training cross-validated AUROC before validation. Performance assessment included bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, calibration, decision curve analysis, and SHAP.
Results: Nine predictors were retained: AKI, T2DM, respiratory rate, lactate, creatinine, BUN, ALT, SOFA, and SAPS II. Stacking ranked first by the training-CV model-selection rule (mean CV AUROC=0.690). AUROC was 0.742 (95% CI 0.690-0.791) in internal validation and 0.633 (0.546-0.718) in external validation. At the locked threshold, external sensitivity was 0.750 and specificity 0.441. The external Brier score of 0.287 exceeded the prevalence-only null Brier score of 0.237 (scaled Brier=-0.212). SOFA alone showed similar external discrimination (AUROC=0.646) with a lower Brier score (0.226), indicating no clear external advantage of the ensemble over simpler benchmarks. Cross-database standardized mean differences demonstrated substantial distribution shift.
Conclusions: The training-selected Stacking model showed moderate internal discrimination but limited external discrimination and probabilistic calibration, without a clear external advantage over simpler benchmarks. The model should be considered investigational pending prospective evaluation and site-specific validation or recalibration.

paper.title: Exploratory evaluation of electroencephalogram-derived features for classification of mild cognitive impairment in two independent datasets.
paper.abstract: A proper diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is one of the important challenges in the early detection of dementia. For the classification of MCI patients and healthy controls, some electroencephalogram (EEG)-derived indices were calculated and compared. Some studies have been conducted on the high accuracy classification of MCI patients and healthy controls, but classification may depend on the dataset and recording conditions. In this study, we evaluated EEG-derived indices in the Japanese and the Iranian EEG datasets and examined their classification performance under within-dataset and cross-dataset validation. This classifier had common features but was learned for each dataset. The Japanese dataset consisted of 7 MCI patients and 10 healthy controls. The Iranian dataset consisted of 29 MCI patients and 32 healthy controls. The common 16 EEG data were separated into 5 frequency bands. Power spectrum and SL values by Synchronization Likelihood were calculated as features for classification. These standardized and exponentially transformed indices were also used as features. Furthermore, graph metrics were calculated based on SL values before or after standardization and exponential transformation. Features used for classification were selected from these indices. The high classification accuracies were obtained from the classifier using a 34-dimensional feature subset selected from standardized and exponentially transformed EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band. Accuracies of this classifier were 88.24% in the Japanese dataset and 86.89% in the Iranian dataset. To evaluate classification accuracy while minimizing information leakage and optimistic bias, nested leave-one-out cross-validation was performed. Accuracies were 88.24% in the Japanese dataset and 83.61% in the Iranian dataset using exponentially transformed EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band. To evaluate whether the classifier can generalize to independent datasets obtained under different recording conditions, exploratory bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation was performed. Accuracies were 40.98% (Training data: the Japanese dataset, Test data: the Iranian dataset) and 58.82% (Training data: the Iranian dataset, Test data: the Japanese dataset). These findings suggested that resting-state EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band may contain information useful for classification of MCI patients and healthy controls. However, they suggested that classifier based on these indices may partly reflect dataset-specific characteristics.

paper.title: TyG-CVAI for identifying hyperuricemia: geographical external validation, model updating, and explainable machine learning.
paper.abstract:
Background: TyG-CVAI can be calculated from routine metabolic and anthropometric measurements, but evidence for same-visit identification of prevalent hyperuricemia across regions, its incremental value beyond conventional variables, and its advantage over the constituent variables themselves remains limited.
Objective: To assess the geographical transportability of the triglyceride-glucose Chinese visceral adiposity index (TyG-CVAI) for identifying prevalent hyperuricemia and to determine whether model updating or more complex machine-learning methods materially improve externally validated performance.
Methods: We analyzed prospectively collected, single-visit health-examination and questionnaire data from 2,119 adults and performed a cross-sectional analysis. The Shandong center was used for model development (n=1,288) and the Jiangsu center for geographical external validation (n=831). Associations were estimated with multivariable logistic regression and robust Poisson regression, with restricted cubic splines for dose-response assessment. Single-index discrimination, transferred thresholds, calibration, decision-curve analysis, five prespecified logistic model formulations, recalibration, reverse validation, and dataset shift were evaluated. Machine-learning models were tuned by nested resampling in Shandong and evaluated once in Jiangsu; serum urate and all outcome-derived variables were excluded from every prediction step.
Results: Hyperuricemia was present in 433 participants (20.43%). A 1-SD increase in TyG-CVAI was associated with higher odds of prevalent hyperuricemia in Shandong (OR, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.39-2.18), Jiangsu (OR, 1.97; 95% CI, 1.50-2.59), and the pooled cohort (OR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.55-2.19), with no center interaction (P = 0.984). The pooled prevalence ratio per 100-unit increase was 1.12 (95% CI, 1.09-1.16). TyG-CVAI AUCs were 0.74 in Shandong and 0.72 in Jiangsu. Applying the rounded Shandong cutoff of 593 in Jiangsu yielded sensitivity 0.75 and specificity 0.52. The external AUC increased from 0.71 for the noncomponent clinical model to 0.74 after adding TyG-CVAI, but a components-only model achieved 0.74 and the clinical-plus-components model 0.76. Penalized logistic regression had the highest external machine-learning AUC point estimate (0.74), but no tree model differed significantly after multiplicity adjustment. The prespecified sex interaction was not significant after Holm correction.
Conclusions: TyG-CVAI was consistently associated with prevalent hyperuricemia across two centers and showed moderate discrimination. It provided a small increment over a clinical model that deliberately excluded its components, but no clear advantage over models using the constituent variables directly. TyG-CVAI may help prioritize direct serum-urate testing when its components are already available, but it should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic or prognostic test.
